teaching.causalExplanation: Start with what Medicare is for. It has two aims. Your ability to get necessary medical care shouldn't depend on your ability to pay. And illness shouldn't ruin you financially. It's paid for from general tax plus an income levy. It isn't a fund you pay into and draw out of. It's today's taxes paying for today's care. That's what universal means here: covered because you live here and need care, not because you contributed or have a job. Now, what does it cover? Inside the boundary: free treatment as a public patient in a public hospital. Rebates for GPs, specialists, tests and scans outside hospital. Medicine subsidy, so you pay a capped amount for listed medicines, less with a concession card. And safety nets, which raise the subsidy once your costs for the year pass a threshold. Outside the boundary: most adult dental care, most physio, psychology and other allied health beyond limited sessions, glasses, ambulances in most states, and private hospital care. That list isn't random. It's exactly where last lesson's out-of-pocket costs pile up. So Medicare is universal for people, but partial for services. How can cost block care in a universal scheme? Government sets a fee and pays a rebate based on it. If a doctor charges that fee and bills Medicare directly, you pay nothing. That's bulk billing. If they charge more, you pay the gap. Say a visit costs ninety dollars and the rebate is forty-two. The gap is forty-eight dollars. The rebate only rises when government decides. If it rises more slowly than the cost of running a practice, the gap grows year after year, with no law ever announcing a fee. It can run the other way, when government lifts rebates or pays more for bulk billing. And it bites hardest on someone with a low income and a chronic condition who needs a visit every month, because twelve visits means five hundred and seventy-six dollars. Then the chain from last lesson runs again.

scenes.teachingReason: How can cost block care in a universal scheme? Government sets a fee and pays a rebate based on it. If a doctor charges that fee and bills Medicare directly, you pay nothing. That's bulk billing. If they charge more, you pay the gap. Say a visit costs ninety dollars and the rebate is forty-two. The gap is forty-eight dollars. The rebate only rises when government decides. If it rises more slowly than the cost of running a practice, the gap grows year after year, with no law ever announcing a fee. It can run the other way, when government lifts rebates or pays more for bulk billing. And it bites hardest on someone with a low income and a chronic condition who needs a visit every month, because twelve visits means five hundred and seventy-six dollars. Then the chain from last lesson runs again.

scenes.teachingReason: What does private health insurance add? It pays for treatment as a private patient, which brings your choice of doctor, your choice of timing, and often a private room. Extras cover helps with dental, glasses and physio. Government encourages it with a premium rebate, a tax penalty for high earners without cover, and higher premiums for late joiners. And community rating means insurers must charge the same premium for the same policy, whatever your health. The case for it: it moves some demand out of public hospitals and brings private money in. The case against: that support goes mostly to people who are better off, and the same money spent on public care could buy more health. Whether it's fair is a value judgement, and saying so is the strong answer.

scenes.teachingReason: Two big programs sit at the edge of Medicare, both funded nationally. The NDIS, the National Disability Insurance Scheme, funds supports for people with permanent and significant disability, through a plan built on the person's own goals. It's not a health scheme. It pays for daily living and independence, not treatment. My Aged Care is the front door to federally funded aged care: an assessment, then help at home or a place in residential care, aiming to keep people at home longer. Both attach funding to the person, not to a service. That fits support to the person's goals, but hands the work of organising providers to the person or their family. And both meet health at a seam, where people wait in hospital for a funded place.

scenes.teachingReason: So what do these arrangements mean for access and equity? Three real gains. Nobody is refused emergency or public hospital care because they can't pay. Medicines stay affordable for life-long conditions. And risk is pooled, so the healthy and the wealthy help pay for the sick and the poor. Three real shortfalls. The services left outside, like dental care, have the steepest gradient. Gaps wear down universal coverage without anyone deciding to. And support for private cover follows income, not need. Which services sit inside the boundary decides who's protected, more than the total spent. And universal coverage doesn't maintain itself.
